name: Lucidchart
tagline: Collaborative flowcharts, system diagrams, and visual documentation

pricing.notes: Working normalization from the official public pricing structure. Recheck the source page immediately before publication.

tiers.name: Individual
tiers.limits: Unlimited editable documents and shapes; 1 GB storage; 1,000+ templates
tiers.notes: Official pages show $9 month-to-month and pricing as low as $7.95/month on annual billing.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Unlimited documents/shapes plus team controls; starts at $9/user/month billed annually
tiers.notes: Exact month-to-month rate and seat minimum were not exposed on the accessible official pricing page.

pricing.hiddenCosts: Taxes are added. Cancellation normally stops the next renewal rather than refunding the current term. Lucidchart, Lucidspark and other Lucid products can be separate subscriptions/add-ons and may each need cancellation; enterprise Accelerators are extra.

verdictSummary: The visible diagramming loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Lucidchart earns its keep through interaction polish, collaboration, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a browser-based diagramming editor with drag, resize, connect, keyboard shortcuts, autosave, and SVG or PNG export.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
whyPeopleStillPay: Lucidchart: The shapes are easy; customers pay for low-friction editing, reliable exports, collaboration, and a canvas that never fights them.
ongoingBurden: Own geometry, selection behavior, undo, clipboard interoperability, export fidelity, accessibility, and browser performance.

priorArt.name: Excalidraw
priorArt.desc: Open-source diagram canvas with an approachable interaction model.

alternatives.name: CryptPad
alternatives.desc: Encrypted collaborative documents, whiteboards, diagrams, slides, and Kanban boards; less polished than Lucidchart, considerably less interested in your data.

facts.install: Use a public CryptPad instance, or self-host the Node.js service behind a reverse proxy
facts.dataFormat: Documents are encrypted in the browser before upload; the server stores encrypted document files, blobs, and account pin metadata on its filesystem and cannot read document content
facts.gapVsPaid: Its diagram tool has far fewer professional shape libraries, templates, imports, data-linking features, and precision controls than Lucidchart.
facts.setupBlocker: Public hosting is immediate; self-hosting requires two domains or subdomains, HTTPS, strict security headers, Node.js configuration, persistent storage, and careful upgrades/backups

alternatives.name: diagrams.net
alternatives.desc: The obvious answer because it is the right one: broad diagramming, local ownership, imports, templates, and real-time collaboration through Google Drive or OneDrive.

facts.install: Open the web app, or install the native desktop package
facts.dataFormat: Diagrams are local .drawio XML files or files saved to a user-selected provider such as Google Drive or OneDrive; the desktop app keeps diagram content on the machine and can export common image/document formats
facts.gapVsPaid: It matches the drawing depth but has a weaker integrated team workspace for comments, review, versioning, administration, and cross-document organization than Lucidchart.

alternatives.name: Excalidraw
alternatives.desc: Faster and friendlier for collaborative sketches and system diagrams; deliberately worse at formal templates and precision drafting.

facts.install: Open the hosted web app/PWA, or deploy the static app and optional collaboration server
facts.dataFormat: Solo drawings are stored in browser storage or explicit .excalidraw JSON files; exports include PNG and SVG; multiplayer room data is end-to-end encrypted and the decryption key is carried in the share URL
facts.gapVsPaid: Its deliberately hand-drawn style, smaller formal-shape library, and limited precision drafting make it much worse for rigorous technical and business diagrams.
facts.setupBlocker: None for the hosted app; the trade-off appears later because durable workspace organization, centralized team administration, and managed version history are deliberately minimal

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Lucidchart is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Lucidchart, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: React + TypeScript + Vite + IndexedDB.
Primary job: Build a browser-based diagramming editor with drag, resize, connect, keyboard shortcuts, autosave, and SVG or PNG export.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: presentation and enterprise controls; multiplayer cursors and comments; large template libraries.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
